title: Tattvārthasūtra

attribution.tradition: Śvetāmbara: Umāsvāti (with his own bhāṣya); Digambara: Umāsvāmin, pupil in Kundakunda's line (also given as Gṛdhrapiccha)
attribution.scholarly: a single author Umāsvāti is generally accepted; his sectarian affiliation and the date are debated

tradition.text: Digambara lineage lists place him soon after Kundakunda

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–5th c. CE (estimates vary; many place it c. 4th–5th c.)

structure.description: 10 chapters; 357 sūtras in the Digambara recension (Sarvārthasiddhi), about 344 in the Śvetāmbara recension (bhāṣya); numbering differs within several chapters

summary: The first Sanskrit summa of Jain doctrine: ten chapters of aphorisms covering the path (the three jewels), knowledge and standpoints (1), the soul (2), the lower and middle worlds (3), the gods (4), the non-soul substances (5), inflow (6), vows (7), bondage (8), stopping and shedding with meditation (9) and liberation (10). Accepted by all Jain sects.

editions.name: Digambara root text, nikkyjain Jain database (local: sources_raw/prepared/tattvartha-sutra)

notes: Śvetāmbara numbering differs from the Digambara (e.g. sallekhanā is Dig 7.22 = Śv 7.17; hiṃsā is Dig 7.13 = Śv 7.8, since the Śv sūtra text lacks Dig 7.4–8; nayas Dig 1.33 = Śv 1.34–35; 'kālaś ca' Dig 5.39 ≈ Śv 5.38 'kālaś cety eke'). Śv numbers given from memory. Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:तत्त्वार्थसूत्र--आचार्य-उमास्वामी); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Tattvārthādhigamabhāṣya

attribution.tradition: Śvetāmbara: Umāsvāti's auto-commentary; Digambara: not by Umāsvāti
attribution.scholarly: many scholars accept it as auto-commentary; others see it as early but separate

scholarly.text: same period as the sūtra or somewhat later (c. 4th–5th c. CE)

summary: Prose commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra that the Śvetāmbaras hold to be Umāsvāti's own (svopajña); it opens with verses on the purpose of the work and closes with a praśasti giving the author's lineage (Uccairnāgara branch) and place of composition (Kusumapura).

title: Sarvārthasiddhi
summary: Pūjyapāda Devanandin's commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra, which fixes the Digambara recension of the sūtras; it expounds the fourteen guṇasthānas under 1.8, argues that sallekhanā is not self-killing (7.22) and reads 9.11 so that the Jina is free of hunger and thirst.
notes: Registry id. The maṅgala verse 'mokṣamārgasya netāraṃ…' is printed at its head (some Digambaras treat it as the sūtra's own invocation).

title: Tattvārtharājavārttika
summary: Akalaṅka's vārttika commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra, which builds on the Sarvārthasiddhi and develops the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī), the division of statement into complete (sakalādeśa) and partial (vikalādeśa), and polemics against other schools.

title: Tattvārthaślokavārttika
summary: Vidyānanda's verse-and-prose commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra, much of it a defence of Jain epistemology and of the omniscient teacher against Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya and Buddhist opponents.

title: Tattvārthabhāṣyavṛtti (Siddhasenagaṇi)
summary: Siddhasenagaṇi's large Śvetāmbara sub-commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra and its bhāṣya.

title: Tattvārthavṛtti (Śrutasāgara)
summary: Late Digambara commentary on the Tattvārthasūtra by Śrutasāgara Sūri.

title: Tattvārthasāra
summary: Amṛtacandra's verse restatement of the content of the Tattvārthasūtra.

title: Āptamīmāṃsā

tradition.text: Digambara tradition: early (often placed in the 2nd c.)

summary: Samantabhadra's 114-verse critical hymn (Devāgamastotra) examining who is a trustworthy teacher (āpta): outward miracles do not prove greatness; the omniscient, faultless teacher is established by reasoning; one-sided (ekānta) views of being and non-being, identity and difference, permanence and momentariness, and monism are refuted by the sevenfold predication, and syādvāda is defined.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आप्त-मीमांसा); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Yuktyanuśāsana
summary: Samantabhadra's hymn to Mahāvīra showing by reasoning that the Jina's doctrine is free of the faults of one-sided views; it calls the Jina's tīrtha 'sarvodaya', the rise of all.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:युक्त्यनुशासन--समंतभद्राचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Svayambhūstotra
summary: Samantabhadra's hymn to the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras (Bṛhat-svayambhūstotra), rich in doctrinal statements; in the Naminātha hymn non-violence is called the supreme Brahman known in the world. Tradition connects its recitation with the appearance of the image of Candraprabha at Vārāṇasī.

title: Ratnakaraṇḍaśrāvakācāra

attribution.scholarly: attribution to the author of the Āptamīmāṃsā is questioned by some

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. CE or somewhat later

summary: The classic Digambara manual of lay conduct (c. 150 verses): right view with its eight limbs, free from three follies and eight kinds of pride; right knowledge (the four anuyogas); the lay vows (five aṇuvratas, three guṇavratas, four śikṣāvratas), the eight basic qualities (mūlaguṇa), sallekhanā with its conditions and faults, and the eleven pratimās.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:रत्नकरण्ड-श्रावकाचार--समन्तभद्राचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date. Verse numbers differ between editions (chapter-wise 1–7 or continuous 1–150).

title: Jinaśataka (Stutividyā)
summary: Samantabhadra's hymn of about one hundred verses to the Jinas written in elaborate figured verse (citrakāvya).

title: Aṣṭaśatī
summary: Akalaṅka's terse commentary ('eight hundred') on the Āptamīmāṃsā, defending omniscience and anekānta against Buddhist logicians.

title: Aṣṭasahasrī
summary: Vidyānanda's large commentary ('eight thousand') on the Āptamīmāṃsā, embedding the Aṣṭaśatī; later commented by Yaśovijaya.

title: Āptaparīkṣā
summary: Vidyānanda's examination of the authoritative teacher, with a sustained refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika Īśvara as creator and as teacher of the path.

title: Sanmatitarka (Sammaisutta)

tradition.text: contemporary of king Vikramāditya of Ujjain

summary: Siddhasena Divākara's Prakrit treatise in three books (kāṇḍa) on the standpoints (nayas), on knowledge and perception (defending their identity in the omniscient), and on the object as substance and modes; it holds that the two root standpoints are the substance-view and the mode-view, that each standpoint taken alone is false and all together true, and that there are as many rival doctrines as there are standpoints. Revered by both sects.
notes: Registry id. Commented by Abhayadeva (Tattvabodhavidhāyinī / Vādamahārṇava). Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:सन्मतितर्क--सिद्धसेनाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Nyāyāvatāra

attribution.scholarly: attribution debated: several scholars ascribe it to a later Siddhasena (Mahāmati) writing after Dharmakīrti

scholarly.text: 5th c. if by Siddhasena Divākara; c. 6th–8th c. if later

summary: A 32-verse manual of Jain logic: valid cognition (pramāṇa) as knowledge illuminating itself and its object without contradiction, perception and inference for oneself and for others, the fallacies, and the place of the standpoints.

title: Dvātriṃśad-dvātriṃśikā
summary: Siddhasena Divākara's 'thirty-two hymns of thirty-two verses' (twenty-one survive): praises of Mahāvīra and critical surveys of the other darśanas (Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Buddhist and others) and of Vedic teaching.

title: Kalyāṇamandirastotra
summary: A 44-verse hymn to Pārśvanātha recited daily and used protectively; the Śvetāmbaras ascribe it to Siddhasena Divākara (the hymn said to have made Pārśva's image emerge from the liṅga at Ujjain), the Digambaras to Kumudacandra.

title: Dvādaśāranayacakra

tradition.text: Prabhāvakacarita: debate at Valabhī in the 4th c.

summary: Mallavādin's 'wheel of standpoints with twelve spokes': twelve philosophical positions (drawn from all the darśanas) are set out so that each refutes the one before it and is refuted by the next; no spoke stands alone, and the whole wheel is the Jain many-sided view. The root text is lost and is reconstructed from Siṃhasūri's commentary.

title: Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī (Siṃhasūri)
summary: Siṃhasūri's commentary on Mallavādin's Dvādaśāranayacakra, through which the lost root text is known.

title: Laghīyastraya
summary: Akalaṅka's 'three small treatises' on valid cognition, standpoints and the fourfold placement (nikṣepa), with his own commentary; it divides direct cognition into the conventionally direct (sense-knowledge) and the truly direct.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:लघीयस्त्रय--भट्टाकलंकदेव); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Nyāyaviniścaya
summary: Akalaṅka's treatise on perception, inference and scripture, written largely against Dharmakīrti.

title: Siddhiviniścaya
summary: Akalaṅka's treatise on the establishment of Jain epistemological and metaphysical positions, preserved with Anantavīrya's commentary.

title: Svarūpasambodhana
summary: A short verse text on the nature of the soul as knower, many-sided and to be realized by oneself; ascribed to Akalaṅka.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:स्वरूप-संबोधन--अकलंक-देव); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Parīkṣāmukha
summary: Māṇikyanandi's sūtra manual of Jain logic in Akalaṅka's system (pramāṇa, its object, its fruit and fallacies).
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:परीक्षामुख); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa
summary: Prabhācandra's large commentary on the Parīkṣāmukha, refuting other schools (including the claim that women can be liberated and that the kevalin eats).
notes: Id already used by another unit (U31); U35 adds its Jain-doctrinal contents.

title: Nyāyakumudacandra
summary: Prabhācandra's commentary on Akalaṅka's Laghīyastraya, with extended polemics (including against the kevalin's eating and women's liberation).

title: Pramāṇanayatattvāloka
summary: Vādidevasūri's Śvetāmbara sūtra manual of logic (pramāṇa and naya), with his own large commentary Syādvādaratnākara.

title: Ālāpapaddhati
summary: Devasena's short manual of the standpoints (naya), substance, qualities and modes.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आलापपद्धति--देवसेनाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya
summary: Jinabhadra Gaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa's great Prakrit verse commentary on the first section (sāmāyika) of the Āvaśyaka, a summa of Śvetāmbara epistemology; it contains the Gaṇadharavāda (Mahāvīra resolving the doubts of the eleven brahmin gaṇadharas on the soul, karma, rebirth, liberation and more) and defends the sequential view of the omniscient's knowledge and perception.

title: Dhyānaśataka (Jhāṇajjhayaṇa)

attribution.scholarly: ascription to Jinabhadra is doubted by some

summary: A Prakrit poem of about 105 gāthās on meditation: the definition of dhyāna as steady mind, the four meditations with their objects, supports, signs and fruits; incorporated into Haribhadra's Āvaśyaka commentary.

title: Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya

tradition.text: Śvetāmbara tradition dates Haribhadra's death to 529 CE

summary: Haribhadra's 228-verse treatise on yoga: three yogas (by desire, by scripture, by capacity), the eight views (dṛṣṭi) — mitrā, tārā, balā, dīprā, sthirā, kāntā, prabhā, parā — each correlated with one of Patañjali's eight limbs, the removal of a fault and the rise of a quality; the unity of the goal under many names; four kinds of yogins.

title: Yogabindu
summary: Haribhadra's Sanskrit treatise (c. 527 verses) on the qualification for yoga (the last turning, caramāvarta; the one who will not again bind the maximum karma, apunarbandhaka), the preliminaries (pūrvasevā), five kinds of religious performance (poison, venom, non-performance, its cause, nectar) and five yogas: adhyātma, bhāvanā, dhyāna, samatā and vṛttisaṃkṣaya.

title: Yogaśataka (Haribhadra)
summary: Haribhadra's Prakrit hundred verses on yoga: yoga in the ultimate sense (niścaya) is the union of the three jewels in the soul, in the conventional sense (vyavahāra) their causes such as serving the teacher; the practitioner's qualification and the teacher's adapting of instruction to the student.

title: Yogaviṃśikā
summary: Haribhadra's twenty Prakrit verses (the 17th of his Viṃśativiṃśikā): all religious activity that joins one to liberation is yoga; its five kinds — posture (sthāna), sound (ūrṇa), meaning (artha), support (ālambana), the supportless (anālambana) — each in four grades (desire, practice, steadiness, perfection). Commented by Yaśovijaya.

title: Viṃśativiṃśikā
summary: Haribhadra's twenty Prakrit sets of twenty verses on doctrine and practice (including the Yogaviṃśikā).

title: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (Haribhadra)
summary: Haribhadra's 87-verse compendium presenting six darśanas — Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā) — each by its deity, categories and means of knowledge, without polemic, adding the Lokāyata at the end for those who count Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika as one. Commented by Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā).
notes: Id already used by U11/U17; U35 adds the Jain view of the other darśanas.

title: Śāstravārtāsamuccaya
summary: Haribhadra's verse examination of rival doctrines (materialism, Buddhism, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Advaita and others), notable for reinterpreting doctrines it rejects in an acceptable sense (e.g. the soul itself as the 'creator' and 'Īśvara'). Commented by Yaśovijaya (Syādvādakalpalatā).

title: Aṣṭakaprakaraṇa
summary: Haribhadra's thirty-two sets of eight verses on Jain practice reinterpreted inwardly: the true Mahādeva is the one free of passion, true bathing and worship are inner, true fire-sacrifice is burning karma; also on alms, food, meditation, austerity and debate.

title: Lokatattvanirṇaya
summary: Haribhadra's verse examination of views about the world and its creation, containing his famous statement that he has no partiality for Mahāvīra nor hatred for Kapila and the others: whoever's word is reasoned should be accepted.

title: Dharmabindu
summary: Haribhadra's sūtra work on the general and particular dharma of householders and ascetics, beginning with the virtues of one who follows the path (mārgānusārin).

title: Anekāntajayapatākā
summary: Haribhadra's major polemical defence of many-sidedness against Buddhist and other one-sided positions, with his own commentary.

title: Ṣoḍaśaka
summary: Haribhadra's sixteen sets of sixteen verses on religious practice, including the four kinds of performance (from affection, devotion, scripture, and without attachment) and the eight defects of mind in practice.

title: Dhūrtākhyāna
summary: Haribhadra's Prakrit satire in which five rogues tell impossible tales and justify them from Purāṇic and epic stories — a critique of uncritical acceptance of myth.

title: Yogaśāstra (Hemacandra)

structure.description: 12 prakāśas, c. 1,000 verses, with the author's own commentary

summary: Hemacandra's treatise in twelve chapters (prakāśa) written for king Kumārapāla: yoga as the three jewels; the conduct and vows of the householder; conquest of the passions and senses, the twelve reflections, equanimity and the four friendly contemplations; postures; breath, the winds and signs of death (with the warning that breath-control does not serve liberation); the four objects of meditation (piṇḍastha, padastha, rūpastha, rūpātīta) with the five concentrations; virtuous and pure meditation; and a closing chapter on his own experience of the no-mind state.

title: Yogaśāstra-svopajñavṛtti
summary: Hemacandra's own long commentary on the Yogaśāstra, with illustrative stories and verses quoted from earlier works.

title: Pramāṇamīmāṃsā
summary: Hemacandra's unfinished sūtra-and-commentary treatise on valid cognition in the Jain system.

title: Vītarāgastotra
summary: Hemacandra's twenty hymns to the passionless Jina, combining devotion with doctrine: obedience to the Jina's command (what to abandon and what to adopt) is higher than worship.

title: Anyayogavyavacchedikā
summary: Hemacandra's 32-verse hymn to Mahāvīra that refutes the doctrines of other schools (creator God, inherence, the Vedic sacrifice, Buddhist momentariness, etc.) and praises the non-partisan many-sided doctrine; commented by Malliṣeṇa (Syādvādamañjarī).

title: Ayogavyavacchedikā
summary: Hemacandra's companion 32-verse hymn establishing the Jina's excellence positively.

title: Syādvādamañjarī
summary: Malliṣeṇa's commentary (1292 CE) on the Anyayogavyavacchedikā, a standard exposition of many-sidedness and of the Jain critique of other schools.

title: Mahādevastotra
summary: A hymn ascribed to Hemacandra, said to have been recited at the Somanātha temple: homage to the one, whether Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara or the Jina, in whom attachment and the other seeds of rebirth are destroyed.

title: Guṇasthānakramāroha
summary: A late Śvetāmbara verse manual on the ascent through the fourteen guṇasthānas and the meditations proper to each.

title: Karmagrantha (the new Karmagranthas of Devendrasūri)
summary: Devendrasūri's Prakrit manuals of karma theory (karma-vipāka, bandha-svāmitva by guṇasthāna, etc.), the standard Śvetāmbara school texts on the kinds, durations and fruition of karma.

title: Navatattvaprakaraṇa
summary: A short Prakrit Śvetāmbara primer on the nine realities (jīva, ajīva, puṇya, pāpa, āsrava, saṃvara, bandha, nirjarā, mokṣa) memorised by students.

title: Lokaprakāśa
summary: Vinayavijaya's encyclopedic Sanskrit verse account (1652) of the Jain universe: substances, souls, the three worlds, time cycles and karma.

title: Bṛhatsaṅgrahaṇī
summary: Śvetāmbara Prakrit manual of cosmology (the classes of beings, their abodes, lifespans and bodies), in versions ascribed to Jinabhadra and to Candrasūri.

title: Jñānārṇava

tradition.text: Śubhacandra was the brother of the yogin Bhartṛhari, in the time of king Bhoja/Muñja of Dhārā

scholarly.text: c. 11th c. CE (relative priority to Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra debated)

summary: Śubhacandra's large Sanskrit treatise on meditation (c. 39–42 sections): the twelve reflections, the meditator and the place, the vows, the conquest of passions, breath-control (with warnings), and the four objects of meditation (piṇḍastha with the five concentrations, padastha on mantras and letters, rūpastha on the Arhat, rūpātīta on the formless Siddha), culminating in pure meditation.
notes: Registry id. Distinct from the Śākta Jñānārṇava-tantra (src:jnanarnava-tantra). Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:ज्ञानार्णव--शुभचंद्राचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Samādhitantra
summary: Pūjyapāda's 105 verses on the three conditions of the self — the outer self that takes the body for the self, the inner self that discerns, and the supreme self — and on abandoning body-identification by discriminative knowledge.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:समाधितन्त्र--आचार्य‌-पूज्यपाद); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Iṣṭopadeśa
summary: Pūjyapāda's 51 verses of 'beneficial instruction': the soul is other than matter, and all further teaching is only the elaboration of that; the practitioner turns from the body and its pleasures to the self.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:इष्टोपदेश--आचार्य‌-पूज्यपाद); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Daśabhakti
summary: Ten devotional hymns (to the Siddhas, scripture, conduct, the yogins, the ācāryas, nirvāṇa and others) used in Digambara liturgy; the Sanskrit set is ascribed to Pūjyapāda.

title: Paramātmaprakāśa

scholarly.text: c. 6th c. CE (some place Yogīndu as late as the 10th c.)

summary: Yogīndu's Apabhraṃśa dohās in two books on the supreme self: the three selves, the soul as in essence the paramātman, the futility of outer practice without self-knowledge, and liberation by knowing the self.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:परमात्मप्रकाश--योगींदुदेव); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Yogasāra (Yogīndu)
summary: Yogīndu's c. 108 Apabhraṃśa dohās on yoga as knowing one's own self to be the supreme self: 'who the supreme self is, that am I'.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:योगसार--योगींदुदेव); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Pāhuḍa Dohā
summary: Rāmasiṃha's Apabhraṃśa dohās criticising outer religion — pilgrimage, temple and image — and locating the Jina in the temple of the body; close in idiom to the Buddhist and later Sant dohās.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पाहुड-दोहा--राम-सिंह-मुनि); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Yogasāraprābhṛta
summary: Amitagati's Sanskrit treatise in nine chapters on the realities and on yoga as the path, closely following Kundakunda.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:योगसार-प्राभृत--अमितगति-आचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Sāmāyikapāṭha (Bhāvanā-dvātriṃśikā)
summary: Amitagati's 32 verses recited in the equanimity practice, opening with the wish to hold friendship for beings, joy in the virtuous, compassion for the afflicted and equanimity toward the perverse.

title: Kārttikeyānuprekṣā (Bārasa-aṇuvekkhā of Svāmi Kārttikeya)
summary: A long Prakrit poem (c. 489 gāthās) on the twelve reflections, which includes a full account of the substances, the world and dharma — defined as the nature of a thing, the ten virtues, the three jewels and the protection of beings.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:वारासाणुवेक्खा--स्वामि-कार्तिकेय); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Dravyasaṃgraha
summary: Nemicandra's 58 Prakrit gāthās summarising the six substances, the seven realities and the path, ending with meditation on the five supreme beings and their mantras of 35, 16, 6, 5, 4, 2 and 1 syllables.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:द्रव्यसंग्रह--नेमिचंद्र-सिद्धांतचक्रवर्ती); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa
summary: Nemicandra's Prakrit compendium on souls, arranged by the fourteen guṇasthānas and the fourteen inquiry-heads (mārgaṇā), including the leśyās with the parable of the six travellers and the fruit tree.
notes: Studied by Banārsīdās with Rūpcand Pāṇḍe (Ardhakathānaka). Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:गोम्मटसार-जीवकांड--नेमिचंद्र-आचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Gommaṭasāra Karmakāṇḍa
summary: Nemicandra's Prakrit compendium on karma: the 148 kinds, bondage, rise, existence and their distribution over the guṇasthānas.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:गोम्मटसार-कर्मकांड--नेमिचंद्र-आचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Labdhisāra
summary: Nemicandra's Prakrit treatise on the attainments (labdhi) that lead to right view and on the ladders of subsidence and destruction.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:लब्धिसार--नेमिचंद्र-आचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Trilokasāra
summary: Nemicandra's Prakrit account of the three worlds (Digambara cosmology and cosmography).

title: Tiloyapaṇṇatti
summary: Yativṛṣabha's Prakrit description of the three worlds, the time cycles and the lives of the Tīrthaṅkaras and other illustrious persons.

title: Mūlācāra
summary: The Digambara Prakrit code of monastic conduct: the twenty-eight basic qualities of the monk (five great vows, five carefulnesses, control of five senses, six essential duties, hair-plucking, nakedness, not bathing, sleeping on the ground, not cleaning the teeth, eating standing, one meal a day), the ten dharmas, reflections and austerities.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:मूलाचार--वट्टकेराचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–6th c. CE (debated); Yāpanīya connections proposed

summary: Śivārya's large Prakrit work on the four propitiations (ārādhanā) — of view, knowledge, conduct and austerity — culminating in the good death: the kinds of death, the conditions for undertaking the fast unto death, the role of the attending teachers (niryāpaka) and the remedies for fear and pain.
notes: Restricted content (fasting unto death): summary and the text's own conditions and warnings only. Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:भगवती-आराधना--शिवाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Ārādhanāsāra
summary: Devasena's Prakrit summary of the four ārādhanās leading to the good death.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आराधनासार--देवसेनाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Tattvasāra (Devasena)
summary: Devasena's short Prakrit text on the self in its own and in the other's nature, meditation and self-realization.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:तत्त्वसार--देवसेनाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Upāsakādhyayana (Somadeva)
summary: Somadeva's manual of lay conduct forming the last books of his Yaśastilaka; it teaches that in worldly (laukika) matters Jains may follow common custom so long as right view is not lost and the vows are not violated.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:उपासकाध्ययन--सोमदेवाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya
summary: Amṛtacandra's 226-verse manual of lay conduct founded on the two standpoints: hiṃsā is the arising of passion in the soul, non-violence its non-arising; the other faults are forms of hiṃsā; sallekhanā undertaken to thin the passions is not self-killing.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पुरुषार्थसिद्ध्युपाय--आ-अमृतचन्द्र); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Ātmakhyāti
summary: Amṛtacandra's Sanskrit commentary on Kundakunda's Samayasāra, which reads the text through the pure standpoint and embeds some 278 verses (the kalaśas).

title: Samayasāra-kalaśa
summary: The c. 278 Sanskrit verses of Amṛtacandra's Ātmakhyāti read as a separate text: on the self shining by self-experience, discriminative knowledge (bhedavijñāna) as the cause of liberation, and the knower who is not the doer. Commented in Hindi by Pāṇḍe Rājamalla (the commentary Banārsīdās read) and by Bhaṭṭāraka Śubhacandra (Parama-adhyātma-taraṅgiṇī).
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:परम-अध्यात्म-तरंगिणी--अमृतचंद्राचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date. (catalogue entry is the kalaśas with a commentary).

title: Tattvapradīpikā (Amṛtacandra on the Pravacanasāra)
summary: Amṛtacandra's commentary on Kundakunda's Pravacanasāra (knowledge, the knowable and conduct; pure, auspicious and inauspicious manifestations of consciousness).

title: Tātparyavṛtti (Jayasena)
summary: Jayasena's commentaries on Kundakunda's Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya, which balance the pure standpoint with the conventional.

title: Ātmānuśāsana
summary: Guṇabhadra's c. 270 verses of self-admonition urging detachment and austerity.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आत्मानुशासन--आ-गुणभद्र); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Padmanandi-pañcaviṃśatikā
summary: Padmanandi's twenty-five short Sanskrit works on the householder's six daily duties, charity, the reflections, the one self (ekatva), and devotion.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पद्मनंदी-पंचविन्शतिका--आ-पद्मनंदी); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Tattvānuśāsana
summary: A Digambara Sanskrit treatise on meditation (dhyāna) as the means to both the conventional and ultimate path; its authorship is given as Nāgasena or Rāmasena.

title: Tattvajñānataraṅgiṇī
summary: Bhaṭṭāraka Jñānabhūṣaṇa's Sanskrit verses on realizing the pure self (śuddha-cidrūpa).
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:तत्त्वज्ञान-तरंगिणी--भट्टारक-ज्ञानभूषण); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Sāgāradharmāmṛta
summary: Paṇḍita Āśādhara's Sanskrit manual of lay conduct (with his own commentary), part of his Dharmāmṛta.

title: Anagāradharmāmṛta
summary: Āśādhara's Sanskrit manual of ascetic conduct, the companion of the Sāgāradharmāmṛta.

title: Vasunandi-śrāvakācāra
summary: Vasunandi's Prakrit manual of lay conduct, organised by the eleven pratimās.

title: Ādipurāṇa (Jinasena)
summary: Jinasena's Sanskrit account of Ṛṣabha and Bharata (first part of the Mahāpurāṇa); its fourth chapter contains a sustained argument against a creator of the world. U35 cites only that argument.
notes: Narrative text in U34's scope; the id is disambiguated from Pampa's Kannada Ādipurāṇa. Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आदिपुराण--जिनसेनाचार्य); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Pañcādhyāyī
summary: Pāṇḍe Rājamalla's unfinished Sanskrit treatise on substance and on right view, organised by the standpoints; an important text of the Adhyātma current.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पंचाध्यायी); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date. (catalogue gives no author).

title: Adhyātmasāra
summary: Yaśovijaya's c. 950-verse Sanskrit work in seven parts on adhyātma: its definition as pure activity centred on the self, the renunciation of hypocrisy, the nature of saṃsāra, three kinds of detachment (born of pain, of delusion, of knowledge), equanimity, right view, yoga as action and knowledge, meditation and self-experience.

title: Adhyātmopaniṣad
summary: Yaśovijaya's Sanskrit verse treatise in four sections on the yoga of scripture, of knowledge, of action and of equanimity, holding knowledge and ritual action together.

title: Jñānasāra
summary: Yaśovijaya's 32 sets of eight Sanskrit verses (256) on the inner path: fullness, absorption, steadiness, renunciation of delusion, knowledge, calm, conquest of the senses, impartiality, fearlessness, self-experience, yoga, worship, meditation, austerity and the refuge of all standpoints.

title: Pātañjalayogasūtravṛtti (Yaśovijaya)
summary: Yaśovijaya's commentary on selected sūtras of Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra, accepting much of Patañjali's method while correcting points of doctrine (the self, Īśvara, liberation) from the Jain many-sided view.

title: Dvātriṃśad-dvātriṃśikā (Yaśovijaya)
summary: Yaśovijaya's thirty-two sets of thirty-two verses, many of them on yoga (including a restatement of Haribhadra's eight views and of Patañjali's system in Jain terms).

title: Adhyātmamataparīkṣā
summary: Yaśovijaya's Prakrit-Sanskrit critique of the Adhyātma movement of Banārsīdās's followers: against its niścaya-only reading and its Digambara positions (e.g. that the kevalin does not eat).

title: Jaina Tarkabhāṣā
summary: Yaśovijaya's manual in three chapters on valid cognition, standpoints and placement (nikṣepa), written in the style of Navya-Nyāya.

title: Jñānabindu
summary: Yaśovijaya's treatise on the five kinds of knowledge, which discusses the sequential, simultaneous and identity views of the omniscient's knowledge and perception and relates them by standpoints.

title: Nayopadeśa
summary: Yaśovijaya's verse treatise on the standpoints, with his own commentary.

title: Syādvādakalpalatā
summary: Yaśovijaya's commentary on Haribhadra's Śāstravārtāsamuccaya.

title: Ānandaghana-aṣṭapadī
summary: Yaśovijaya's eight Gujarati/Hindi verses in praise of Ānandaghana, which the tradition takes as a record of their meeting.

title: Ānandaghana Covīsī
summary: Ānandaghana's hymns (stavana) to the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in old Gujarati-Rajasthani (he completed twenty-two; later poets supplied the last two): the soul's love-longing for the Jina as its only beloved, the difficulty of the true path, and the six darśanas as the limbs of the Jina.
notes: Language given as old Gujarati-Rajasthani (Marugurjara). Commented by Jñānavimala and by Śrīmad Rājacandra's circle (recalled).

title: Ānandaghana Bahottarī
summary: Seventy-two (more in some collections) devotional-mystical padas in old Hindi attributed to Ānandaghana: the avadhūta who knows the self beyond sects and names, the soul-bride awaiting her lord, and inner experience (anubhava).
notes: Attribution of individual padas varies between collections (low confidence on any given pada).

title: Devacandra Covīsī
summary: Devacandra's Gujarati hymns to the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, noted for their dense Jain philosophical content.

title: Adhyātmagītā (Devacandra)
summary: Devacandra's Gujarati poem on the self's return to its own nature.

title: Yuktiprabodha
summary: Meghavijaya's Śvetāmbara refutation of the 'Vāṇārasīya' (Banārsīdās's Adhyātma) doctrine.

title: Cidānanda Bahottarī
summary: Seventy-two Hindi padas of the Śvetāmbara mystic Cidānanda (Kapūrcand) on the self and detachment.

title: Svarodaya (Cidānanda)
summary: A Hindi verse work ascribed to Cidānanda on the science of the breath through the nostrils (svara) as an omen and aid to practice.

title: Samayasāra Nāṭaka
summary: Banārsīdās's Braj Hindi verse rendering (1636) of the Samayasāra as read through Amṛtacandra's kalaśas and Rājamalla's commentary, cast as a drama of the self (cetana) and non-self; its closing chapter on the fourteen guṇasthānas is the author's own addition.
notes: Chapter structure follows the Samayasāra's adhikāras plus Banārsīdās's additions (details low confidence). Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:समयसार-नाटक); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Ardhakathānaka
summary: Banārsīdās's Braj Hindi verse autobiography (1641) of the first fifty-five years of his life — 'half' of a full span — including his religious wanderings, his fall into a one-sided niścaya view after reading the Samayasāra, and his recovery of balance when taught the guṇasthānas by Rūpcand Pāṇḍe.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:अर्धकथानक--बनारसीदास); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Banārasīvilāsa
summary: The collection of Banārsīdās's shorter Hindi works (hymns, adhyātma poems, translations) compiled after his death (1644).

title: Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka
summary: Ṭoḍarmal's unfinished Hindi prose treatise on the path to liberation: wrong views (including one-sided niścaya and one-sided vyavahāra), the nature of karma and the true path; a foundational text of the Digambara Terāpantha.

title: Chahḍhālā
summary: Daulatrām's Hindi primer in six 'ḍhāl' songs (1834) on the suffering of the four destinies, wrong and right view, the vows, the twelve reflections and the path to liberation; widely memorised.

title: Ātmasiddhi Śāstra
summary: Śrīmad Rājacandra's 142 Gujarati dohās (1896) establishing the six fundamentals — the soul exists, is eternal, is the doer and the enjoyer of its karma, liberation exists and there is a means to it — with the marks of the true teacher (sadguru) and of the sectarian (matārthī) and the self-seeker (ātmārthī).
notes: Registry id. Tradition: written in one sitting for Saubhāgbhāī and a few close disciples.

title: Apūrva Avasara
summary: Śrīmad Rājacandra's Gujarati poem (c. 1896–97) longing for the 'unprecedented occasion' of becoming free of all knots, outer and inner, and describing the ascent to omniscience and liberation.

title: Mokṣamāḷā
summary: Śrīmad Rājacandra's 108 short Gujarati lessons on Jain doctrine and conduct, written at about sixteen.

title: Namaskāra-mantra (Navakāra, Pañca-parameṣṭhi-namaskāra)
alt_titles: Pañcamaṅgala-mahāśrutaskandha (Śvetāmbara name for the mantra with cūlikā)

attribution.scholarly: the five homages appear at the opening of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Bhagavatī; an early form of the first homages occurs in Khāravela's Hāthīgumphā inscription

structure.description: 5 lines of homage (35 syllables) + 4-line cūlikā (33 syllables) = 68 syllables in 9 lines (Śvetāmbara)

summary: The fundamental Jain mantra in Prakrit: homage to the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Ācāryas, the Upādhyāyas and all Sādhus in the world; the Śvetāmbara form adds a four-line cūlikā declaring that this fivefold homage destroys all evil and is the first of all auspicious things.

title: Uvasaggaharaṃ-stotra

attribution.tradition: Bhadrabāhu (Śrutakevalin or the later Bhadrabāhu, brother of Varāhamihira)

summary: A five-verse Prakrit hymn to Pārśvanātha, 'remover of calamities', recited daily for protection; the tradition ascribes it to Bhadrabāhu, composed to protect the community from the vengeful spirit of his brother Varāhamihira.

title: Bhaktāmara-stotra
summary: Mānatuṅga's Sanskrit hymn to Ṛṣabha — 44 verses in the Śvetāmbara text, 48 in the Digambara — recited by all Jains; the tradition tells that each verse broke a fetter when the king imprisoned the poet. A later tradition attaches a mantra, a yantra and a benefit to each verse.

title: Ṛṣimaṇḍala-stotra
summary: A protective hymn and its yantra centred on the seed 'hrīṃ' and the syllables of the five supreme beings, with the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras; ascribed by tradition to Gautama Gaṇadhara.

title: Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa
summary: Malliṣeṇa's Sanskrit manual (ten chapters) of the worship and mantras of the goddess Padmāvatī, attendant of Pārśvanātha: the qualities of the practitioner, protection of the body, worship of the goddess, yantras, and rites for worldly ends (pacifying, attracting, subjugating, immobilising, and the curing of snake-poison).
notes: Restricted: summary only; no mantras, yantras or rites reproduced.

title: Jvālāmālinī-kalpa
summary: Indranandi's Sanskrit manual (939 CE) of the worship and mantras of the goddess Jvālāmālinī, attendant of Candraprabha.

title: Mantrarājarahasya
summary: Siṃhatilaka Sūri's Sanskrit work (13th c.) on the Sūrimantra, the secret mantra of the Śvetāmbara ācāryas, and its practice.
notes: The Sūrimantra itself is transmitted orally to ācāryas at installation; its wording is not recorded here.

title: Sūrimantrabṛhatkalpavivaraṇa
summary: Jinaprabha Sūri's account of the Sūrimantra's divisions, presiding deities and practice.
